The lighthouse had been Elias's for eleven years. Eleven years of winding the clockwork, polishing the great Fresnel lens, and watching the fog roll in like a slow gray tide that swallowed the world whole. He liked it that way. The fog meant no one was coming. No one to ask why he'd left Margot, why he'd traded a house in Dunmore for a tower of white stone at the edge of the Croagh Head. No one to notice the way his hands shook when the winter gales turned the sea into something that roared.

On the morning the bottle came, the fog had thinned to a pale gauze, and Elias was on the rocks below the tower, collecting driftwood for the stove. The tide had pulled back further than it had in weeks, exposing a shelf of black basalt slick with kelp. He was prying a hunk of barnacled log free when his fingers closed around something smooth and cold.

A bottle. Green glass, the neck sealed with a waxy cork that had swollen with years of salt. He pried it open with his thumbnail, the wax cracking with a sound like a small bone breaking. Inside, a rolled piece of paper, darkened to the color of weak tea.

He sat down on the wet rock, the November wind cutting through his oilskin, and unrolled the paper. The handwriting was small, slanted, urgent.
